items.title: [Atlas Obscura] Tuam Railway Station in Tuam, Ireland
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Tuam Railway Station opened in 1860 as part of the Waterford, Limerick and Western Railway, becoming one of the most important railway hubs in the west of Ireland.

Passenger services ended in 1976 as part of a nationwide rationalisation of the railway network, although freight trains continued to use the station until 1993.

Since then, the station has stood largely abandoned, with its Victorian buildings gradually falling into disrepair. Despite this, many original features—including the distinctive wrought-iron lattice footbridge, platform canopies, goods facilities, and water tower—still survive, making Tuam one of Ireland's most complete surviving historic railway stations.

There have been proposals to restore the railway as part of the Western Rail Corridor, but the station remains closed today.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Protecting our FLOSS commons from LLMs
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Bastian Greshake Tzovaras, Otto Richter, William Zijl, Codeberg News, Jul 24, 2026

Codeberg is a software repository site, a lot like GitHub but without the Microsoft business model. It made news this week by taking measures against AI-generated code, aka 'vide coding'. I'm not really a fan of the 'deny AI' response, but this document is reasonable and well argued, targeted against the abuses AI creates. For example: "At Codeberg, we are happy to provide free and open access to code. Just run git clone and enjoy. Unfortunately, these crawlers instead try to read every single page from Codeberg, no matter if it makes sense... These needless accesses create expensive database queries that diminish the service quality for all of us." Also, they're not trying to hunt down every instance of AI use, and will likely discourage but tolerate "side projects and experiments with little resource usage" and "specific tools and custom scripts that would be unlikely to find a community anyway, even if they were not LLM-generated."

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Fossils discovered in Japan more than two decades ago have finally been identified as a new genus and species of giant salamander. Limnospondylus ajimuensis lived around 3.5 million years ago in a warmer, wetter Kyushu and may have reached 1.1 meters in length. Its discovery hints that many more unknown giant salamanders could be hiding among fossils previously given the wrong classification.

items.title: [Atlas Obscura] The Afro-Antillean Museum in Panama City, Panama
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

During the construction of the Panama Canal hundreds of thousands of workers were imported from Jamaica and other Caribbean islands and were settled in tenement housing on the outskirts of Panama City.

Each house was constructed as small as possible, often no more than a wooden shack raised on posts to keep the insects out, with communal bathrooms and a zinc roof. It was in one of these tenement neighbourhoods, known then as Guachapalí, today as El Marañón, that canal workers constructed the Cristian Mission Chapel in their off hours, from 1909-1910.

Countless church services, weddings, funerals and baptisms were performed there, and those worshiping inside would have experienced and withstood the post-canal deportation schemes, denials of citizenship, and attempts at cultural erasure imposed on their community, as well as the eventual governmental recognition of their rights and way of life.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Night owls and early birds
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

As young kids, most of us were up at 6 am, raring to go on weekend mornings. As teenagers, many of us slept in until late morning or noon. But people are different. Some love Marmite, some hate it. As adults, we start finding what works best for us. And it’s not necessarily the same as, or what works best for, our partners.

It struck me that I know a lot of couples, us included, who are night-owl/early-bird combos.

One of the couple naturally wakes at dawn and tiptoes out of bed. They’ve usually managed a host of morning peaceful time, exercise or chores before the night owl surfaces, often bleary-eyed.

And while the early bird crashes out in the evening, maybe falling asleep on the sofa, the night owl is often just getting going, hitting their productive stride, staying out, or watching late-night TV, before tiptoeing into bed next to the sleeping early bird.

Of course, we notice and talk about the differences. So perhaps there are a host of early-bird couples and night-owl couples. But eventually we all settle into the rhythms that work best for us, and I’m pretty sure I see a lot of opposites.

I can’t help wishing I were naturally an early bird on the same schedule as my wife. But perhaps it’s a combo that creates time for both partners and secretly a recipe for success?

As Kahlil Gibran wrote in The Prophet:

"And stand together yet not too near together:

  For the pillars of the temple stand apart,

  And the oak tree and the cypress grow not in each other's shadow."

Are you a night owl living with an early bird, or vice versa? How do you make it work for you?
